RTX 5090 prebuilts — desktops, servers, laptops

Every RTX 5090 machine in the sweep (716 listings), cheapest first, grouped by category. A 5090 desktop is rated at 1,792 GB/s of memory bandwidth (32GB GDDR7, 512-bit) — above the 1 TB/s floor. The laptop 5090 is a different chip: 896 GB/s (24GB GDDR7, 256-bit), so no laptop reaches 1 TB/s on GPU bandwidth. These do not appear in the ranked tables: at $2.60/GB·s a 5090 desktop cannot beat a $1.77/GB·s cut, so the ranking hides them by design.

Method, and what got dropped

Every row is a live listing. Prices, availability text and the buy link were read off the retailer's own search/listing page over a real browser session on 2026-10-13; the link goes to the product page, not to a search results page. Nothing here is a price estimate, a cached price, or a modelled build.

$/GB·s = price ÷ the GPU's published memory bandwidth in GB/s. Bandwidth comes from a cited spec table (159 GPU rows, 109 CPU rows, 23 server platforms, 26 iGPU parts — every row carries source URLs in deals/spec_gpu_bw.json and deals/spec_mem_bw.json). A machine with no discrete GPU (servers, iGPU mini-PCs) is scored on system memory bandwidth, channels × MT/s × 8 ÷ 1000, from the CPU/platform row. Laptop listings are matched to laptop GPU rows — a 5090 laptop is 896 GB/s, not the desktop's 1,792, and the table uses the laptop number. Portability is read from the listing, not from the search that found it: a ZBook Fury or Dell Precision mobile workstation is scored on the laptop part, and a desktop tower naming a "1TB GEN4" SSD is not.

Known approximation. Where a GPU model has no separate laptop row in the spec table — the Pascal and Turing mobile parts (GTX 1060/1070/1080, GTX 1650/1660, RTX 2060/2070/2080) — the laptop listing is scored on the desktop figure. That is accurate for these: NVIDIA's mobile variants of those generations keep the same bus width and memory speed, so the bandwidth is the same. It is not true for Ampere and later, which is why those generations do have separate rows.

$/GB RAM and $/GB Sto divide the same price by the RAM and storage the listing states. A listing that does not state RAM or storage is dropped rather than shown with a blank denominator — we never divide by a number we did not read.

Buy-now gate. A card is only listed when its own card text shows a way to buy it now (in stock, add to cart, ships in N days, N available). Out-of-stock, sold-out, pre-order and "see all buying options" cards are dropped. Price ranges and "from" prices are dropped too, because a range has no single number to divide by. eBay queries are restricted to Buy It Now so every eBay row is an instant purchase, not an auction.

What got screened out — 28,401 of 37,498 cards:
Drop reasonCards
RAM not stated in title9,326
no bandwidth basis (no GPU/CPU/platform match)6,230
storage not stated in title5,806
price below $150 (not a whole machine)1,748
no machine word in title1,724
bare part: motherboard311
bare part: bezel264
accessory: compatible with233
bare part: graphics card222
bare part: power supply187
Read the price as a snapshot. These are retail listings: stock, price and configuration move within hours, and a marketplace seller can change a listing after the scrape. The buy link is the check — open it before treating any row as a deal. Refurbished and open-box rows are labelled in the listing sub-line so they are never mistaken for new.
Reproduce: python deals/deals_scrape.py --site all --cat all (writes deals/raw_*.jsonl), then python deals/deals_score.py (writes deals/scored.json + deals/dropped.json), then python report_deals.py. Spec tables: deals/spec_gpu_bw.json, deals/spec_mem_bw.json. Generated 2026-10-13 21:33.
